questions.question: What are emulsions? Discuss the applications of emulsions in medicine and cleansing action of soap. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What are emulsions? Discuss the applications of emulsions in medicine and cleansing action of soap.
  • An emulsion is a colloidal system of two immiscible liquids in which one liquid acts as the dispersed phase
  • while the other liquid acts as the dispersion medium. Two types Oil in water type and water in oil type.
  • Medicines
  • In medicines Colloidal system is used as therapeutic agents in different areas. Example: -Silver colloids as
  • germicidal agents
  • Copper colloids as anticancer drugs. (i) Colloidal dispersion of gelatin is used in coating over tablets and
  • granules which upon drying leaves a uniform dry film over them and protect them from adverse conditions
  • of the atmosphere.
  • Targeted drug delivery: Targeted drug delivery system is a special form of drug delivery system where the
  • medicament is selectively targeted or delivered only to its site of action or absorption and not to the non-
  • target organs or tissues or cells. Colloidal systems are used as the targeted drug delivery system.
  • Cleansing action of soap
  • The way soap removes dirt and grease is a classic example of emulsification. Dirt is usually oily, and since
  • water and oil don't mix, water alone can’t be used to clean. A soap molecule has two distinct ends:
  • Hydrophilic Head: Water-loving and polar and Hydrophobic Tail: Water-fearing and non-polar (usually a long
  • hydrocarbon chain). When we apply soap to greasy hands, the hydrophobic tails "dive" into the oil/grease,
  • while the hydrophilic heads stay pointing out toward the water. The soap molecules surround the oil
  • droplet, forming a spherical structure called a micelle. The oil is trapped in the centre. As we scrub,
  • emulsification happens and these micelles are lifted off the surface. Because the outer layer of every micelle
  • is negatively charged (the heads), they repel each other. This prevents the oil droplets from clumping back
  • together.
  • (Definition 2 marks, Application in medicine - 3 marks, Cleansing action of soap- 5 marks)

questions.question: Write a short note of the following a) Hardy-Schulz rule b) electrical double layer / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Write a short note of the following a) Hardy-Schulz rule b) electrical double layer
  • (a) The greater the valency of the flocculating ion added, the greater is its power to cause precipitation. This is
  • known as Hardy-Schulze rule.
  • The coagulating power increases with the valency of an ion.
  • For example, in the coagulation of a negative sol, the order of flocculating power can be depicted as:
  • Al 3+ > Ba 2+ >Na+
  • Similarly, in the coagulation of a positive sol, the order of flocculating power can be depicted as:
  • (5 marks)
  • (b) The electrical double layer is a structure that forms at the interface between a charged surface (such as a
  • colloidal particle or electrode) and a surrounding liquid containing ions. It consists of two layers of opposite
  • charges, which play a crucial role in the stability and behaviour of colloidal systems. The first layer is fixed
  • (Stern layer) and the second layer is mobile which is called diffused layer (Gouy- Chapmann layer). Potential
  • difference of this electrical double layer is called Zeta
  • potential(Z).
  • (5 marks)

questions.question: Explain the principle, instrumentation, and working of potentiometric titration. Discuss the role of indicator electrode and reference electrode with suitable examples. / [CO4] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the principle, instrumentation, and working of potentiometric titration. Discuss the role of indicator
  • electrode and reference electrode with suitable examples
  • Potentiometric titration is a volumetric method in which the potential difference between two electrodes is
  • measured as a function of the added titrant volume. The principle rests on the Nernst Equation, which
  • relates the electrode potential to the concentration of the species in the solution:
  • Instrumentation- 3 main components
  • • Reference Electrode: An electrode with a constant, known potential (e.g., Saturated Calomel Electrode or
  • Ag/AgCl electrode).
  • • Indicator Electrode: An electrode whose potential depends on the concentration of the analyte (e.g., Glass
  • electrode for pH, Platinum wire for redox).
  • • Potentiometer/pH Meter: To measure the potential difference between the two electrodes.
  • Working
  • • The analyte solution is taken in a beaker.
  • • The indicator electrode and reference electrode are immersed in the solution.
  • • The titrant is added gradually from the burette.
  • • After each addition, the potential difference (E) is measured.
  • • A graph is plotted between: Potential (E) vs Volume of titrant, or ΔE/ΔV vs Volume (for sharper
  • endpoint detection).
  • • The equivalence point is identified from the sharp jump in potential or peak in derivative curve.
  • Indicator electrode responds to the activity (concentration) of the analyte ion and reference electrode
  • maintains a constant potential regardless of solution composition. For example, in case of acid- base titration
  • indicator electrode is Glass electrode and reference electrode is Calomel electrode.
  • (Principle- 2 marks, Instrumentation- 3 marks, working - 3 marks, Electrodes explanation- 2 marks)
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026
